name: Supply Chain Security
intent: Treat the code and tooling you depend on as an attack surface: control which versions you run, verify what you downloaded, and decide how fast to adopt updates.
scenario: A web app has about 400 transitive dependencies. A popular package, three levels down, ships a malicious patch release on day 10 after its maintainer's account is taken over. It is yanked on day 15. One build pipeline floats on ^1.2.0, another uses a lockfile with a weekly update bot.
problem: You run far more code than you wrote or reviewed, and each dependency is a stranger with publish rights. An attacker does not need to break into you: a phished maintainer, a typosquatted name, an internal package name that also exists publicly, an install script, or a compromised build server is enough. Vulnerability scanners only know attacks that already have a CVE, so a brand-new malicious release looks clean to them. And patching fast, which you want for known CVEs, is the same behaviour that pulls a malicious release in the first hours.

howItWorks.title: Know what you actually run
howItWorks.text: A version range like ^1.2.0 means >=1.2.0 <2.0.0, so any new 1.x release is adopted by the next unpinned install, including a malicious one. A lockfile (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, go.sum) records the exact version, the source URL and an integrity hash (for example sha512 or sha256) for every transitive package, so the same commit builds the same tree. Install with the frozen mode (npm ci, pip --require-hashes, go with -mod=readonly) so CI fails instead of silently re-resolving. An SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) is the exported inventory of that tree, so on the day an advisory lands you can answer 'do we run it, and where?' in minutes.

howItWorks.title: Close the naming and routing holes
howItWorks.text: Typosquatting relies on a mistyped name (reqeusts). Dependency confusion relies on a resolver that searches several registries and takes the highest version: the attacker publishes your internal name acme-billing 99.0.0 publicly and wins. Fix it by routing: scoped names (@acme/billing) mapped to your private registry only, or a single virtual registry that proxies the public one and blocks names that exist internally. A lockfile also stops it until the next re-resolution, which is why routing is the real fix.

howItWorks.title: Verify the bytes, and limit what install can do
howItWorks.text: Integrity hashes catch bytes that changed after the lock was written, such as a swapped tarball on a mirror or CDN. They do not catch a malicious release the maintainer published properly, because the hash you record is the hash of the bad file. Many attacks execute at install time through preinstall or postinstall scripts, with the CI runner's tokens in the environment, so disable lifecycle scripts by default (npm --ignore-scripts, pnpm's build allowlist) and run installs without deploy credentials.

howItWorks.title: Choose an update policy on purpose
howItWorks.text: Floating ranges adopt everything immediately. A lockfile plus a bot (Dependabot, Renovate) adopts on a schedule. Exact pins plus human review adopt rarely. A minimum release age (Renovate minimumReleaseAge, pnpm minimumReleaseAge, uv exclude-newer) refuses versions younger than, say, 3 to 7 days. Most malicious releases are caught and yanked within hours to a few days, so a short cooldown avoids most of them. The price is that real security fixes wait too, so keep an explicit fast path for versions that fix a known CVE.

howItWorks.title: Scan for known problems, and do not trust the scan for new ones
howItWorks.text: Software composition analysis (npm audit, OSV-Scanner, Trivy, Grype) matches your SBOM against advisory databases of known CVEs. That finds old, disclosed flaws and tells you which fix to take. It cannot flag a malicious release nobody has reported yet, and it says nothing about whether a package is trustworthy. Pair it with behaviour checks (new install script, new network call, maintainer change) from tools such as Socket or an internal diff review for high-risk packages.

howItWorks.title: Prove where your own artifacts came from
howItWorks.text: Build on hardened, ephemeral runners from reviewed source, then sign the result and attach provenance: Sigstore (cosign, keyless signing with short-lived certificates logged in Rekor) and an in-toto/SLSA provenance statement saying which repo, commit and builder produced the artifact. SLSA levels rise from documented provenance (L1), to a hosted build that signs it (L2), to a hardened build where a run cannot tamper with its own provenance (L3). Admission control then refuses images without a valid signature. Reproducible builds let a second party rebuild the source and compare hashes, so a compromised build server is detectable. Prefer minimal base images (distroless, scratch) so there is less third-party code to inherit and patch.

pros: Lockfiles with hashes make builds repeatable and turn silent changes into reviewable diffs
Scoped registries remove dependency confusion entirely instead of making it less likely
A short release-age cooldown avoids most malicious releases at almost no engineering cost
SBOMs and provenance turn 'are we affected?' from a day of grepping into a query
cons: Every defence that delays adoption also delays real security fixes
Lockfile and integrity checks do not help against a malicious release you chose to adopt
Scanners lag behind attackers: they only see what has already been reported
Signing and provenance prove where an artifact came from, not that the source was benign
Reviewing diffs of hundreds of transitive packages is not realistic for a normal team
whenToUse: Any production service built from public packages, which is nearly all of them
Anything with CI credentials, signing keys or cloud deploy roles reachable from the build
Organisations with internal package names or a private registry
Software you ship to customers, where you are someone else's supply chain
whenNotToUse: Full SLSA L3 hermetic builds and reproducibility for a throwaway internal tool: the cost is not matched by the risk
Hand-reviewing every dependency diff: spend that effort on the few packages with install scripts, native code or broad privileges
A long release-age cooldown on security-fix updates: wait for ordinary releases, not for CVE fixes
Relying on a vulnerability scanner as the control for malicious packages
pitfalls: Pinning direct dependencies exactly but leaving transitive ones floating because there is no lockfile or it is not used in CI
Running npm install in CI instead of npm ci, which rewrites the lockfile and re-resolves ranges
A bot that auto-merges updates the moment CI is green, so the lockfile is just a delayed floating range
Scoped registry rules written for @acme/* while old unscoped internal names remain resolvable from the public registry
Regenerating the whole lockfile to fix a merge conflict, which silently adopts every newer version
Yanking a version does not remove it from lockfiles or caches that already hold it: you still have to find and replace it
Giving the install step production or publish tokens, so a postinstall script can exfiltrate them
Signing artifacts but never verifying the signature at deploy time

roles.label: Attacker
roles.description: Controls a maintainer account or a lookalike package and publishes the malicious version.

roles.label: Package registry
roles.description: Serves versions and hashes; can yank a release and publish advisories.

roles.label: CVE scanner
roles.description: Matches your dependency list against known advisories; blind to unreported attacks.

roles.label: Build pipeline
roles.description: Resolves and installs dependencies, either floating or from a lockfile with hashes.
